candidate_relations.reason: Hip MRI and isotope bone scan found no osteonecrotic lesion despite progressive pain.
Impaired mobility and chronic illness could cause deconditioning, but rising inflammatory markers and bilateral iliopsoas edema indicate an active inflammatory syndrome.
A single urinary-incontinence episode prompted spinal evaluation, but it neither persisted nor explains the pelvic-girdle inflammation.
MRI showed bilateral iliacus and iliopsoas inflammation rather than focal sciatic irritation by the piriformis muscle.
Hip aspiration was unsuccessful and colchicine did not relieve symptoms, leaving no crystal proof for gouty arthropathy.
Bilateral iliopsoas and iliacus edema documents inflammatory muscle-region involvement, but treating it as idiopathic misses the elderly-onset systemic PMR diagnosis.
Chronic disease may contribute to weakness, yet the focal decline tracked worsening pain and inflammatory markers rather than generalized deconditioning.
MRI and bone scanning showed no osseous infection while blood and urine infection workup was unrevealing.
Chronic kidney disease complicated admission with pre-renal injury but does not explain the bilateral pelvic-girdle inflammatory MRI pattern.
The initial blood pressure of 88/45 mmHg corrected with fluids and is not the cause of persistent hip pain and raised ESR and CRP.
Advanced age, progressive pelvic-girdle pain, rising ESR and CRP, and bilateral iliopsoas-region inflammation support polymyalgia rheumatica.
MRI showed bilateral muscle edema without a drainable collection, and sepsis investigations did not reveal an infectious source.
Lumbar MRI found only mild L5–S1 foraminal narrowing with no central canal stenosis to explain the deficits.
Bilateral enhancement occurred without a focal collection, fever, bacteremia, or creatine-kinase elevation supporting pyomyositis.
The small hip effusion could not be aspirated and empiric colchicine failed, so gouty arthritis was not established.
The low blood pressure responded to intravenous fluid without ongoing vasopressor-dependent shock, unlike the persistent inflammatory pain syndrome.
Urgent lumbar MRI showed neither central canal compression nor an epidural lesion compatible with cauda equina syndrome.
Although gout was in the history, no tophi, erosions, or crystal demonstration linked chronic gout to the hip presentation.
Left hip and knee weakness worsened alongside severe pain, but weakness alone does not encode the inflammatory PMR cause.
Dedicated hip and pelvic imaging did not show femoral or pelvic osteomyelitis despite elevated inflammatory markers.
